prime.problem: Reading about LLMs leaves you able to trace a model but not write one, and two good resources pull in different directions: Raschka's book codes the whole pipeline at toy scale, while Zero to Hero goes deep on fewer pieces. Without a route you either switch between codebases or skip the depth that makes the code make sense.
prime.fits: The map for the Build an LLM path. It builds on the LLM basics course (the route a question takes through a trained model) and lays the book's chapters over five days, with the Zero to Hero courses and this course's three cards beside them.
expect: the book as the spine: appendix A, chapters 2–7, appendices D and E
Zero to Hero as depth: courses 2 and 3 on the path, 8, 9 and 10 optional
a gap card for training pairs, instruction tuning and LoRA
what a toy-scale GPT-2 leaves out at real scale
prime.goal: Say what you build on each of the five days, which card to reread before each chapter, and which Zero to Hero course to open when a chapter leaves you with a specific question.

attend: Why do Zero to Hero 2 and 3 come before the first language-model chapter, rather than after it?
Which chapters does each gap card prepare, and what does the book do quickly there?
Why is the validation loss on Day 4 expected to stall, and what does the path do about it?
Which Zero to Hero courses are optional, and what specific gap in the book does each one fill?
What would change if you pretrained at real scale instead of on one short story?

must: The book's chapters build on each other's code → one codebase grows from a training loop (Day 1) to GPT-2 124M (Day 3) to a fine-tuned assistant (Day 5) → keep the book as the spine and code it in order

The book lets PyTorch compute gradients and uses a ready-made tokenizer → those are the parts you'd otherwise only trust → Zero to Hero 2 (backprop by hand) and 9 (train a tokenizer) fill exactly those gaps

Pretraining on a 5,145-token story for several epochs → the model memorises it and validation loss stalls after epoch 2 → the book loads OpenAI's weights (§5.5), and Zero to Hero 10 shows real pretraining on about 10 billion tokens

Each gap card measures an idea the book codes quickly → you know what a correct batch, mask or parameter count looks like before you write it → read the card the evening before, code the chapter with it closed
reference: Day 1: appendix A · Day 2: ch 2–3 · Day 3: ch 4 · Day 4: ch 5 + appendix D · Day 5: ch 6–7 + appendix E
the book's code: github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch, one folder per chapter
Zero to Hero 10: 19,073 steps of 2<sup>19</sup> tokens of FineWeb-Edu

compress.prompt: Close the page and draw the five days as a spine of boxes. In each, write the chapters and what runs at the end of the day; beside it, the card or Zero to Hero course that plugs in, marked core or optional.
checklist: Day 1: appendix A, with Zero to Hero 2 and 3 on the path
Day 2: ch 2–3, the training-pairs card, Zero to Hero 9 optional
Day 3: ch 4, GPT-2 124M, Zero to Hero 8 as an optional second pass
Day 4: ch 5 + appendix D, overfitting a short story, Zero to Hero 10 as the stretch
Day 5: ch 6–7 + appendix E, the instruction-tuning and LoRA cards, then the checkpoint

retrieve.q: Explain why this path follows the book's chapter order and treats Zero to Hero as optional depth, rather than the other way round.
answer: the book is linear: each chapter's code builds on the last, ending at an assistant
it runs on a laptop, so every day ends with something that works
Zero to Hero's last course ends at a pretrained GPT-2: no classifier, instruction tuning or LoRA
its depth (backprop, tokenizer training, GPU pretraining) answers questions the book leaves open

retrieve.q: Walk through what you have running at the end of each of the five days.
answer: Day 1: a PyTorch training loop, and a trained bigram model
Day 2: a data loader of (input, target) batches and multi-head causal attention
Day 3: an untrained GPT-2 124M that generates gibberish
Day 4: a model trained on a short story, then GPT-2 with OpenAI's weights
Day 5: a spam classifier, an instruction-tuned assistant scored by a judge, and a LoRA version

retrieve.q: You have one spare day in the week. Spend it on Zero to Hero 9 (tokenizer), 8 (second pass at GPT) or 10 (real pretraining). Pick one for a reader whose chapter 4 code works but who couldn't explain it, and say what they give up.
answer: course 8: it rebuilds the same model from another angle, which targets 'works but can't explain'
course 9 only matters if tokenization is the confusing part
course 10 needs rented GPUs and assumes chapter 4 is already understood
giving up: no hands-on tokenizer, and no feel for training at scale

compare.q: The LLM basics map follows one question through a trained model; this map follows the book through five days of building. What does each order make easy, and when would you go back to the other?
answer: basics is data-flow order: the order a trained model uses its parts, good for reading and debugging
this path is build order: the order training needs the parts
go back to the basics map when your code's shapes or outputs don't match a real model's

compare.q: Zero to Hero 8 and Raschka chapter 4 build the same kind of GPT. What differs in how they get there, and which would you use first?
answer: Karpathy builds up live on Shakespeare characters, from a bigram baseline
Raschka builds GPT-2's exact shape with its tokenizer, so OpenAI's weights load into it later
use the book first on this path; course 8 as a second pass if chapter 4 felt like copying

predict.q: Swap the book's 5,145-token story for a text 1,000 times longer and train for the same number of steps. What happens to the gap between training and validation loss, and would you still load OpenAI's weights afterwards? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: The model sees far fewer repeats of each passage, so it has less chance to memorise: the gap between training and validation loss shrinks, and the book notes that training on 60,000 Project Gutenberg books doesn't overfit (§5.2 note). You'd still load OpenAI's weights for a useful model: a few million tokens on a laptop is nowhere near the scale GPT-2 was trained at. The path didn't measure this run.

apply.task: Before Day 3, predict what your chapter 4 model will print. GPT-2 124M has a 50,257-token vocabulary and width 768. Work out how many weights the output layer adds if it isn't tied to the embedding table, and what the total is with tying, given an untied total of 163,009,536.
apply.done: You have 50,257 × 768 = 38,597,376 for the output layer, and 163,009,536 − 38,597,376 = 124,412,160 with tying: the 124M in the name. Your chapter 4 code should print the 163,009,536.
apply.hint: Tying means the output layer reuses the embedding table, so its weights are counted once.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how much text the book pretrains on, or what happens to validation loss?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the depth options sit where they do?
